topic: How engineers saved the Leaning Tower of Pisa
title: Touch It Wrong, It Falls
hook_promise: How do you straighten a tower that could fall if you touch it wrong?

hook_options.line: Touch it wrong, it falls. Now fix it.
hook_options.frame_one: The host stands at dusk before the leaning tower, one hand reaching out to touch it, frozen mid-reach with a worried look.
hook_options.answer: Carefully taking soil from beneath the north side lets the tower settle and straighten.
hook_options.loop_line: Touch it wrong, and it falls. Touch it carefully, and you fix it.

hook_options.line: How do you straighten a leaning tower?
hook_options.frame_one: The host stands beside the tilting tower holding a plumb line up to it, head tilted to match the lean.
hook_options.answer: You remove soil from under the north side, carefully, and let the tower settle back.
hook_options.loop_line: Carefully, soil by soil, that is how you straighten a leaning tower.

hook_options.line: One wrong move, and the tower falls.
hook_options.frame_one: The host tiptoes toward the base of the leaning tower, then freezes with a foot in the air as the tower looms above.
hook_options.answer: The right move was underexcavation: removing soil under the north side so it settled.
hook_options.loop_line: One careful move at a time, and the tower stands.

storylines.title: Touch It Wrong, It Falls
storylines.hook: Touch it wrong, it falls. Now fix it.
storylines.pitch: The tower could fall, and the wrong move could bring it down. Lead weights on the north side bought time, but a 1995 attempt to replace them made its southward movement speed up, and safety cables went on. The fix that worked: carefully removing soil from beneath the north side.
storylines.conflict: The lean had to be reduced, but working on the tower or its ground could make it fall.
storylines.stakes: First, lead counterweights on the north side. Then the 1995 attempt to replace them with ground anchors failed and the southward movement sped up ("Black September"). Safety cables were added before the final work.
storylines.twist: The answer was underexcavation: removing small amounts of soil from beneath the north side so it settled.
storylines.payoff: How do you fix it? Take soil out from under the high north side, a little at a time, and let it settle back.
visuals: The leaning tower at dusk, the host reaching out and freezing
Lead counterweights stacked at the base of the north side
The 1995 near-disaster: an urgent night scene at the tower, the host jolts
Steel cables around the tower, the host holds a coil of cable
Cutaway of the foundation with soil drawn out from under the north side
Split screen: 1995 near-disaster vs the slow, careful fix

storylines.title: Myth: They Propped Up the Low Side
storylines.hook: Everyone thinks they propped it up. Wrong.
storylines.pitch: Most people assume engineers saved the tower by strengthening the side that sinks. In fact the south side was too risky to disturb, so they removed soil from the north side and let it sink. Cables stood guard the whole time, and the tower ended up 38 cm straighter.
storylines.conflict: The obvious fix, reinforcing the low south side, was judged too dangerous.
storylines.stakes: The myth sounds sensible, but the real job was riskier, so cables had to be installed before any digging started.
storylines.twist: The tower was straightened by taking soil away from the north side, not by adding support to the south.
storylines.payoff: The real fix was cleverer than the myth: it let the tower pull itself back toward vertical.
visuals: Split screen: 'Myth' with host holding a prop under the south side, 'Fact' with soil removed from the north
Painted tower on soft ground with a buried riverbed below
Close-up of cables tightened one by one
Host holds a small scoop of soil and points at the north side

storylines.title: You're One of the 13 Experts
storylines.hook: You're one of 13 experts. Fix this tower.
storylines.pitch: It's 1990 and the tower leans 5.5 degrees, built on soft silt since 1173. You can't touch the south side, so you must take soil out from the north side. You rig cables first, dig carefully for years, and the tower ends up 38 cm straighter.
storylines.conflict: You have to reduce the tilt, but any disturbance to the ground under the south side is too dangerous.
storylines.stakes: The usual fixes are off the table, the only plan is risky, and you must install cables to stop any unwanted movement before you start.
storylines.twist: The plan is to remove soil under the high north side, so the tower settles back toward vertical.
storylines.payoff: From 1993 to 2001 the work cuts the tilt to 3.97 degrees, answering the call to fix the tower.
visuals: Host in a committee room, camera pushes in on a drawing of the tower
Painted map pin on Pisa with 1173 and 1990 labels
Host holds a cable and tightens it
Close-up of the foundation with small amounts of soil removed from the north side
Final scene: host stands small beside the tower, 38 cm label

sources.claim: Engineering analyses found the tower's safety margin against falling over was very low, with a factor of safety of only 1.07 to 1.15.
sources.title: Jamiolkowski (2001), The leaning tower of Pisa: End of an Odyssey, ISSMGE conference proceedings
sources.quote: its factor against falling over is very low and falls in the range of 1.07 to 1.15

sources.claim: In the second half of 1993, 600 tonnes of lead weights were placed on the north side of the foundations, on a removable concrete ring cast around the base of the tower.
sources.title: Burland, Jamiolkowski & Viggiani (2009), Leaning Tower of Pisa: behaviour after stabilization operations, ISSMGE Int. J. of Geoengineering Case Histories 1(3)
sources.quote: Temporary stabilisation of the foundation was achieved during the second half of 1993 by the application of 600t of lead weights on the north side of the foundations via a post-tensioned removable concrete ring cast around the base of the Tower at plinth level

sources.claim: The lead counterweight, placed between May 1993 and January 1994, made the tower reverse the direction of its movement for the first time in its history.
sources.title: Jamiolkowski (2001), The leaning tower of Pisa: End of an Odyssey, ISSMGE conference proceedings
sources.quote: The counterweight placed in the period between May 1993 and January 1994, produced a very positive response of the monument, which, for the first time in its history, inverted the direction of the movement

sources.claim: In September 1995, during an unsuccessful attempt to replace the lead weights with temporary ground anchors, the tower's southward movements accelerated, and the lead load was raised to 900 tonnes to control them; this period is called "Black September".
sources.title: Burland, Jamiolkowski & Viggiani (2009), Leaning Tower of Pisa: behaviour after stabilization operations, ISSMGE Int. J. of Geoengineering Case Histories 1(3)
sources.quote: In September 1995 the load was increased to 900t in order to control the accelerating southward movements of the Tower during an unsuccessful attempt to replace the unsightly lead weights with temporary ground anchors. This difficult period during the Committee's activity has been called "Black September"

sources.claim: While part of the ground structure around the south of the base was being removed to build a concrete ring for the anchors, the tower began tilting south at 3 to 4 arc-seconds per day, with serious concern for its stability.
sources.title: Jamiolkowski (2001), The leaning tower of Pisa: End of an Odyssey, ISSMGE conference proceedings
sources.quote: During the first attempt to remove in small segments the South part of the catino to build the prestressed concrete ring for the ten anchors, the Tower started to tilt towards South at a rate of 3" to 4" per day with serious concern for its stability

sources.claim: Before the final stabilisation works, a safeguard of cables was attached to the tower to prevent any unexpected movement; it was never needed and was never put into operation.
sources.title: Jamiolkowski (2001), The leaning tower of Pisa: End of an Odyssey, ISSMGE conference proceedings
sources.quote: before starting the final stabilisation works under the Tower, to prevent any unexpected adverse movement during this intervention, a safeguard structure was implemented consisting in a cable stay ... Providentially, the underexcavation interventions did not require the use of the safeguard structure so that the cable stay was never put into operation

sources.claim: The fix was underexcavation: highly controlled extraction of ground from beneath the north side, which made the north edge settle and reduced the tower's inclination by one tenth of its 1993 maximum.
sources.title: Jamiolkowski (2001), The leaning tower of Pisa: End of an Odyssey, ISSMGE conference proceedings
sources.quote: The method chosen to stabilise the Tower consisted in highly controlled ground extraction, named underexcavation, which by inducing the settlement of the North edge of the plinth, allowed to reduce the inclination of the Tower by 1800 arc-seconds, one tenth of the maximum tilt, recorded in 1993

sources.claim: 38 cubic metres of soil were removed from underneath the raised end of the tower to slightly straighten it by 45 centimetres, returning it to a position last seen in 1838.
sources.title: Imperial College London news (2011): Prof. who helped save Leaning Tower of Pisa
sources.quote: which saw 38 cubic metres of soil removed from underneath the raised end of the tower to slightly straighten it by 45 centimetres, returning the tower to a position previously seen in 1838

sources.claim: In March 1990, Professor John Burland of Imperial College London was asked to join a 14-member committee charged with stabilising the tower.
sources.title: Imperial College London news (2011): Prof. who helped save Leaning Tower of Pisa
sources.quote: In March 1990, Professor Burland was asked to be part of a 14 member committee charged with stabilising the tower
